stories.headline: The Hidden Epidemic
stories.title: The Hidden Epidemic
stories.summary: The Kashmir Care Foundation (KCF) and the Gauri Kaul Foundation (GKF) recently convened a conversation that involved physicians and public health experts for an interactive session titled “The Quadruple Problem of Our Times: Fatty Liver Disease, Diabetes, Cardiovascular Disease, and Acute & Chronic Kidney Disease.” The title sounds clinical. But the problem it describes isn’t distant or abstract—it’s at our dinner tables, in our salted noon chai (in Kashmir), in oily foods, in the large portions we eat, in sedentary lifestyles (especially in winter), and increasingly, in our children. These four conditions are usually discussed as separate diseases, treated by separate specialists, in separate hospital wards, and at different times in our lives. But they share the same roots, feed off one another, and, encouragingly, respond to many of the same fixes. Understanding them together, as one interconnected picture, is the first step to actually doing something about them. The session led to the launch of a KCF and GKF Wellness Hour Series (Sehat Nama), where we organise sessions grounded in clinical science and public health and guided by experts. A Regional Crisis, not a Hypothetical One The numbers from Jammu and Kashmir over the past two years should worry every household. • Surging Diabetes Rates: The National Family Health Survey (NFHS-6, 2023-24) found that 13% of women and 11.3% of men in J&K now have high blood sugar or take medication for it — up sharply from 8.7% and 8% in NFHS-5. Urban areas fare even worse, reaching 17% among urban women and 14.6% among urban men. Nearly 40% of all diabetes cases in the region remain completely undiagnosed. • The Jammu Spike: The landmark ICMR-INDIAB national study revealed an overall diabetes prevalence in Jammu of 18.9% (climbing to an alarming 26.5% in urban pockets), with an additional 10.8% living with prediabetes. • Escalating Hypertension: Regional studies place blood pressure prevalence among men in J&K around 25% and women near 12%, surging to over 41% in some tribal communities. Districts like Rajouri and Anantnag recorded some of the highest blood pressure rates in the country. • Silent Liver Damage: While solid local data remains limited, Kashmiri hepatologists report rising rates of Fatty Liver Disease, with ultrasound studies identifying the condition even in schoolchildren. Local clinical estimates run as high as 30% of adults. • The Quiet Fourth Partner: Kidney disease rarely announces itself with dramatic symptoms until function is significantly lost. This makes unmanaged diabetes and hypertension particularly dangerous in a region where both are widespread. Why Jammu & Kashmir Is Uniquely Vulnerable These numbers are rising faster here than in many other parts of the country due to specific cultural, lifestyle, and regional factors: • Dietary Shifts: Traditional Kashmiri, Dogra, and other North Indian diets—once built around seasonal vegetables, dried greens, walnuts, and modest portions of meat—have shifted toward rich, red-meat-heavy Wazwan preparations (in Kashmir), often consumed daily with plenty of rice and bread. Vegetable, salad and fruit consumption is rather low • High Salt Consumption: Salted, buttered noon chai is a major, often overlooked source of daily sodium intake directly linked to the region’s high hypertension burden. • Winter Inactivity: Long, harsh winters discourage outdoor physical activity for months at a time. • Substance Use & Painkillers: Smoking and recreational drug use add strain on the heart, liver, and kidneys. Meanwhile, unsupervised overuse of over-the-counter NSAID painkillers for cold-weather joint pain quietly damages kidney function over years. • Genetic Susceptibility: Well-documented genetic predispositions in Kashmiri, Dogra, Gujjar, and Bakerwal populations mean even modest weight gain can lead to metabolic disease faster. One Chain, Four Links The panel stressed that these four conditions are interconnected rather than isolated: Fatty liver disease is now recognized as the hepatic face of the same insulin resistance and obesity that drive diabetes. High blood pressure damages both the heart’s arteries and the kidneys’ filtering units. A patient who develops one of these four conditions faces a significantly elevated risk of developing the other three. Conversely, controlling one condition well helps protect against the rest. Eight Actionable Steps Families Can Take Now 1. Make Exercise a routine: Exercise for 30-45 minutes a day, and challenge yourself to lose 5% of your weight in the next 3 months and 10% in 6 months. Make it a routine. A BMI between 18.5 and 24.9 is considered the “healthy” or “normal” range for most adults. This is the target to reach. 2. Get Screened Without Symptoms: Fasting blood sugar, blood pressure, lipid profiles, routine kidney/liver function tests, and albumin excretion testing are the only ways to catch silent conditions early. 3. Rethink Salt Intake: Cut back on added salt in tea, cooking, and traditional winter preparations (salted, smoked, or pickled foods). 4. Keep Moving in Winter: Adopt indoor walking, stretching, and simple home exercise routines during the snowy months. 5. Reserve Wazwan for Special Occasions: Return to treating heavy feasts as occasional events, prioritizing vegetables, pulses, whole grains, and fish for daily meals. 6. Use Painkillers Cautiously: Avoid frequent, unsupervised use of OTC painkillers for joint and muscle pain to protect kidney health. 7. Address Substance Use Early: Deploy school- and community-level education to combat smoking, alcohol, and drug use before metabolic damage occurs. 8. No to smoking and alcohol: This is non-negotiable and should become a prime driver for safe health and living. A Call for Integrated Public Health Action A single evening session cannot reverse health trends built over decades. However, initiatives by the Kashmir Care Foundation and Gauri Kaul Foundation help bring these four interconnected diseases into public focus. Government hospitals and primary health centres across both Jammu and Kashmir divisions can launch integrated screening camps. Checking blood sugar, blood pressure, liver markers, and kidney function in a single visit will prove vital for high-risk rural and tribal communities. Masjids, Gurdwaras, Temples, and Churches should share public health messages through a physician member of the congregation, so people are regularly made aware of prevention and advocacy messages they can use to improve their health. The data is unambiguous. The response must match it — in our clinics, in our schools, in our places of worship, and in our workplaces and homes. Authors: Upendra Kaul, New Delhi, India Abdul Hamid Zargar, Srinagar, India Showkat Ali Zargar, Srinagar, India Subhash Wangnoo, New Delhi, India Vijay Kher, New Delhi, India Altaf Lal, Atlanta, USA

stories.headline: Govt Teachers Can Be Deployed As BLOs For Election-Related Duties, Including SIR Work: Allahabad High Court
stories.title: Govt Teachers Can Be Deployed As BLOs For Election-Related Duties, Including SIR Work: Allahabad High Court
stories.summary: HC says BLO duties fall within the RTE Act's exception permitting teachers to be deployed for election-related work.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: HC says BLO duties fall within the RTE Act's exception permitting teachers to be deployed for election-related work.
The Allahabad High Court has observed that government teachers can be assigned election-related duties as Booth Level.
Officers (BLOs), including work pertaining to preparation, revision and correction of electoral rolls.

A bench of Justice Vinod Diwakar referred to Section 27 of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 (RTE Act), which expressly permits the deployment of teachers for election-related duties and that BLO duties fall within this exception.

Rejecting the petitioners' contention that their deployment violated Article 21-A of the Constitution, the bench said the petitioners failed to show that their assignment as BLOs prejudiced their teaching duties or the education of children.
Briefly put, the petition was filed by 5 Assistant Teachers working at Junior/Senior Basic Schools in Saharanpur.
They sought a direction to the authorities to detach them from their duties as BLOs and restrain them from interfering with their discharge of duties as teachers.
It was their contention that there was no provision in the terms and conditions of their service under which they could be assigned BLO duties.

They further argued that such deployment was contrary to Article 21-A of the Constitution, read with the provisions of the RTE Act and the Rules framed thereunder, as it diverted teachers from their core duty of imparting education.
Finding no merits in the petition, the Court noted that the preparation and revision of electoral rolls is a statutory function under the Representation of the People Act, 1950.
It further observed that Article 324 of the Constitution vests the superintendence, direction and control of elections in the Election Commission of India.

The Court also referred to Section 13CC of the 1950 Act, under which officers and staff of the State Government and local authorities employed in the preparation, revision and correction of electoral rolls are deemed to be on deputation to the Election Commission for that period.

stories.headline: Delhi building collapse: Death toll rises to 3, another worker's body recovered
stories.title: Delhi building collapse: Death toll rises to 3, another worker's body recovered
stories.summary: Five people have been pulled out of the rubble; police book owners and contractors for culpable homicide
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'building collapse' in title weight 46
article_sentences: - Death toll in Old Delhi building collapse rises to three after another labourer's body is recovered.
- Five people rescued so far, including two injured workers who are stable.
- Police book building owners and contractors for culpable homicide; unauthorised construction had been flagged in June.

The death toll in the three-storey building collapse in Old Delhi's Hauz Qazi area rose to three on Saturday, 7 November after rescuers recovered the body of another worker from the debris, nearly 48 hours after the incident.
The deceased has been identified as Pankaj Sharma (40), a resident of Hanuman Nagar village in Bihar's Khagaria district, officials said.
Five people have so far been pulled out of the rubble — three dead and two injured.
Both survivors have received medical treatment and are reported to be stable.
Rescue operations and efforts to clear the debris were continuing at the site.
The under-construction building collapsed in Gali Sitara, near Chawri Bazar Metro station, around 9.45 am on Thursday, 5 November.
Between 10 and 15 labourers were present at the construction site when the three-storey structure came crashing down, deputy commissioner of police (central) Rohit Rajbir Singh had said.
Earlier, two labourers identified as Kishori (40) and Sanjeet (45) were declared dead.
Two others, Sahdev Chaudhary (25) and Firoz (37), were rescued with injuries.

stories.summary: The Supreme Court permitted the bursting of certified green firecrackers between 6 a.m. and 7 a.m. and between 8 p.m. and 10 p.m. on November 7 and November 8, 2026 in Delhi-NCR

article_sentences: The Supreme Court on November 2, 2026 described bursting of firecrackers during Deepavali as a “religious practice” while permitting the use of green firecrackers for two days, on November 7 and November 8, in Delhi-NCR.

The unregulated use of firecrackers during Deepavali has historically led to a sharp rise in the Air Quality Index (AQI) and pollution levels, including the emission of particulate matter, the court observed.

“The right of an individual to engage in a particular practice, which may have a religious colour, is only a qualified one and cannot go beyond the Constitutional restrictions,” the Supreme Court held.
The state had “utterly failed” to comply with the Supreme Court’s orders issued since 2015 to impose restrictions on fireworks, the Bench said.
In fact, the situation had not improved even after the reimposition of a complete ban on firecrackers.
A significant spike in AQI levels was noticed on Dasara and the following day.
The “complete ban” had not only facilitated the illegal sale of firecrackers but had also prevented people from purchasing authorised green crackers, the court said.
The court had earlier suggested that the government enlist celebrities such as cricketer Virat Kohli to spread awareness about the harmful effects of firecrackers.

In October 2025, the apex court had permitted the sale and bursting of green firecrackers in Delhi-NCR during Deepavali, subject to conditions aimed at balancing tradition with environmental and health concerns.
The court had then made it clear that the use of green crackers would be restricted to specified hours on the festival day and its eve.

The court permitted the bursting of certified green firecrackers between 6 a.m. and 7 a.m. and between 8 p.m. and 10 p.m. on November 7, 2026 and the day after in the Delhi National Capital Region (Delhi-NCR).
“There shall not be any bursting of fireworks within a 300-metre radius of hospitals, nursing homes, primary and district health centres, old age homes and any notified silence zones.

stories.headline: Maldivian President Pushes for Revival of SAARC
stories.title: Maldivian President Pushes for Revival of SAARC
stories.summary: The President of the Maldives, Mohammed Muizzu, made another call for the revival of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) during his visit to Pakistan on October 21, 2026. Bangladesh, under Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, has also called for the revival of SAARC. The idea has received support from experts and public intellectuals concerned about the welfare of people living in the region. The Government of India responded to these remarks by stating that Pakistan was “stymieing” the grouping. The Promotion of BIMSTEC as an alternative to SAARC is an exercise in diplomatic shortsightedness. Equally shortsighted is the idea of reviving SAARC without India. Countries in the region have little to lose but much to gain if the SAARC platform is revived. The 19th SAARC Summit was scheduled to be hosted in Islamabad from November 15 to 19, 2016, but was indefinitely postponed amid escalating tensions between India and Pakistan. On the positive side, however, relations between India and Pakistan have not completely broken down on all fronts. India’s External Affairs Minister, S. Jaishankar, visited Pakistan on October 15–16, 2024, to attend the 23rd meeting of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Council of Heads of Government and thanked Pakistan for its hospitality. India also participated in the planning session of the SCO Council of National Coordinators in Islamabad from September 28 to 30, 2026.The two countries completed their 35th consecutive exchange of lists of nuclear installations and facilities on January 1, 2026. The hotlines between the Directors General of Military Operations (DGMOs) remain active, and the ceasefire is also holding. Furthermore, the statement made by RSS leader Dattatreya Hosabale on improving people-to-people contact between India and Pakistan was a welcome development. Many experts consider the RSS as India’s deeper state, influencing relations with Pakistan. Be that as it may, three immediate factors have a bearing on the revival of SAARC. Weighing Three Factors First, the dominant view in India is that containing terrorism emanating from Pakistan is the magic bullet for rescuing bilateral relations and bringing them back to normalcy. Diplomat Ajay Bisaria argues that “India’s instincts were primarily economic, and India’s relationship with its neighbours was focused on providing security for the Indian economy to grow and preserving the economic gains already made.” This is quite understandable and reasonable for any major economy but is not exclusive to India. This instinct is now fairly widespread across the countries of the region. There is a growing consensus that terrorism poses a threat to the social and economic stability of countries and that SAARC, as a regional forum, can be employed to combat it. According to the think tank PISCES, Pakistan alone witnessed 225 militant attacks in a single year up to September 2026. Therefore, the way forward lies in greater cooperation among states and a deeper process of introspection within societies. Second, the China factor is also influencing the prospects for the growth and revival of SAARC. China enjoys observer status in SAARC, while India has opposed its full membership of the organisation. India’s unilateral military actions have prompted Pakistan to seek even greater strategic proximity to China, particularly through the acquisition of Chinese military equipment and technology. The clashes between India and Pakistan in May laid bare the consequences of this policy. One consequence of such a scenario is that India’s strategic autonomy in the region is constrained, resulting in the ceding of strategic space to China. There are indications that Pakistan is signalling to both the United States and China that it no longer wishes to be a “client state”. In 2022, Pakistan released its first-ever “National Security Policy”, which emphasised that the country should resist joining geopolitical camps. The weakening of the pro-India lobby in Pakistan is also a matter of concern. Third, there are sections of opinion in Pakistan that believe India will always prefer to engage with a weak Pakistan rather than the Pakistan that exists today. Former Pakistan High Commissioner to India Abdul Basit recently claimed at a seminar in Pakistan that the country’s international profile had risen and that India would therefore prefer disengagement. Some India watchers in Pakistan also point to unilateralism in India’s domestic and regional politics, along with its alleged disregard for international norms and agreements, as factors contributing to growing mistrust. In light of the above discussion, it is important to examine the perspectives of the scholarly community on the challenges confronting South Asia. Scholars Speak Friend and colleague, Happymon Jacob, who has considerable expertise in Indian foreign policy, argues in his essay, “The End of South Asia: A Region in Name Only,” published in Foreign Affairs on July 22, 2024, that the dream of South Asia as a cohesive region is over, with significant implications for subcontinental geopolitics that policymakers and analysts have yet to fully grasp. He writes that the reality of India’s centrality has meant that New Delhi does not always recognise the value of building regional structures, as such structures cannot add much to the predominance India already enjoys in the region. Although several Indian Prime Ministers have recognised the merits of SAARC, the Indian bureaucracy and strategic establishment have never been fully convinced of its value. They have long feared that the creation of regional structures could potentially constrain India’s dominance in its neighbourhood. Nepal-based scholar Kanak Mani Dixit, finds Jacob’s thesis problematic for more than one reason. He believes that Jacob’s pronouncement on the death of South Asia appears to serve the interests of “nation-statism”, which cannot adequately manage the vast geography and multiplicity of identities that characterise South Asia. Mr Dixit further argues that Jacob’s views will please those who wish to exercise centralised authority, ranging from generals in Islamabad to autocratic politicians in Kabul and Colombo, as well as dominant lobbies in New Delhi. True South Asian regionalism has not evolved to a point where the nation-state can function to the satisfaction of the people living in the region. However, we are yet to find an effective institutional mechanism to address inter-state disputes. It would therefore be incorrect to argue that regionalism in South Asia can begin or end with SAARC. The two need to be differentiated. The late Prime Minister Dr Manmohan Singh’s longing for a day when he could have breakfast in Amritsar, lunch in Lahore and dinner in Kabul remains a compelling vision and is not beyond achievement. The precondition for realising this vision is that people’s power must be unleashed and mobilised in the service of humane regionalism in South Asia. The corporate sector, too, is not averse to such thinking. At one-point, Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee nominated R.K. Mishra, a former journalist and a close associate of Dhirubhai Ambani, who headed the Reliance conglomerate. body: The idea has received support from experts and public intellectuals concerned about the welfare of people living in the region.
The Government of India responded to these remarks by stating that Pakistan was “stymieing” the grouping.
The Promotion of BIMSTEC as an alternative to SAARC is an exercise in diplomatic shortsightedness.
Equally shortsighted is the idea of reviving SAARC without India.
Countries in the region have little to lose but much to gain if the SAARC platform is revived.
The 19th SAARC Summit was scheduled to be hosted in Islamabad from November 15 to 19, 2016, but was indefinitely postponed amid escalating tensions between India and Pakistan.
On the positive side, however, relations between India and Pakistan have not completely broken down on all fronts.

India’s External Affairs Minister, S. Jaishankar, visited Pakistan on October 15–16, 2024, to attend the 23rd meeting of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Council of Heads of Government and thanked Pakistan for its hospitality.
India also participated in the planning session of the SCO Council of National Coordinators in Islamabad from September 28 to 30, 2026.
The two countries completed their 35th consecutive exchange of lists of nuclear installations and facilities on January 1, 2026.
The hotlines between the Directors General of Military Operations (DGMOs) remain active, and the ceasefire is also holding.
Furthermore, the statement made by RSS leader Dattatreya Hosabale on improving people-to-people contact between India and Pakistan was a welcome development.
Many experts consider the RSS as India’s deeper state, influencing relations with Pakistan.
Be that as it may, three immediate factors have a bearing on the revival of SAARC.
Weighing.
Three Factors First, the dominant view in India is that containing terrorism emanating from Pakistan is the magic bullet for rescuing bilateral relations and bringing them back to normalcy.

Diplomat Ajay Bisaria argues that “India’s instincts were primarily economic, and India’s relationship with its neighbours was focused on providing security for the Indian economy to grow and preserving the economic gains already made.” This is quite understandable and reasonable for any major economy but is not exclusive to India.
This instinct is now fairly widespread across the countries of the region.
There is a growing consensus that terrorism poses a threat to the social and economic stability of countries and that SAARC, as a regional forum, can be employed to combat it.
According to the think tank PISCES, Pakistan alone witnessed 225 militant attacks in a single year up to September 2026.
Therefore, the way forward lies in greater cooperation among states and a deeper process of introspection within societies.
Second, the China factor is also influencing the prospects for the growth and revival of SAARC.
China enjoys observer status in SAARC, while India has opposed its full membership of the organisation.
India’s unilateral military actions have prompted Pakistan to seek even greater strategic proximity to China, particularly through the acquisition of Chinese military equipment and technology.
The clashes between India and Pakistan in May laid bare the consequences of this policy.
One consequence of such a scenario is that India’s strategic autonomy in the region is constrained, resulting in the ceding of strategic space to China.
There are indications that Pakistan is signalling to both the United States and China that it no longer wishes to be a “client state”.
In 2022, Pakistan released its first-ever “National Security Policy”, which emphasised that the country should resist joining geopolitical camps.
The weakening of the pro-India lobby in Pakistan is also a matter of concern.
Third, there are sections of opinion in Pakistan that believe India will always prefer to engage with a weak Pakistan rather than the Pakistan that exists today.

Former Pakistan High Commissioner to India Abdul Basit recently claimed at a seminar in Pakistan that the country’s international profile had risen and that India would therefore prefer disengagement.

Some India watchers in Pakistan also point to unilateralism in India’s domestic and regional politics, along with its alleged disregard for international norms and agreements, as factors contributing to growing mistrust.
In light of the above discussion, it is important to examine the perspectives of the scholarly community on the challenges confronting South Asia.

Scholars Speak Friend and colleague, Happymon Jacob, who has considerable expertise in Indian foreign policy, argues in his essay, “The End of South Asia: A Region in Name Only,” published in Foreign Affairs on July 22, 2024, that the dream of South Asia as a cohesive region is over, with significant implications for subcontinental geopolitics that policymakers and analysts have yet to fully grasp.

He writes that the reality of India’s centrality has meant that New Delhi does not always recognise the value of building regional structures, as such structures cannot add much to the predominance India already enjoys in the region.
Although several Indian Prime Ministers have recognised the merits of SAARC, the Indian bureaucracy and strategic establishment have never been fully convinced of its value.
They have long feared that the creation of regional structures could potentially constrain India’s dominance in its neighbourhood.
Nepal-based scholar Kanak Mani Dixit, finds Jacob’s thesis problematic for more than one reason.

He believes that Jacob’s pronouncement on the death of South Asia appears to serve the interests of “nation-statism”, which cannot adequately manage the vast geography and multiplicity of identities that characterise South Asia.

Mr Dixit further argues that Jacob’s views will please those who wish to exercise centralised authority, ranging from generals in Islamabad to autocratic politicians in Kabul and Colombo, as well as dominant lobbies in New Delhi.
True South Asian regionalism has not evolved to a point where the nation-state can function to the satisfaction of the people living in the region.
However, we are yet to find an effective institutional mechanism to address inter-state disputes.
It would therefore be incorrect to argue that regionalism in South Asia can begin or end with SAARC.
The two need to be differentiated.
The late Prime Minister Dr Manmohan Singh’s longing for a day when he could have breakfast in Amritsar, lunch in Lahore and dinner in Kabul remains a compelling vision and is not beyond achievement.
The precondition for realising this vision is that people’s power must be unleashed and mobilised in the service of humane regionalism in South Asia.
The corporate sector, too, is not averse to such thinking.
At one-point, Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee nominated R.K. Mishra, a former journalist and a close associate of Dhirubhai Ambani, who headed the Reliance conglomerate.
Reliance had an additional stake in India-Pakistan peace, as it had invested in a refinery in Jamnagar, Gujarat, close to the Pakistan border.
Against this backdrop, it needs to be emphasised that the absence of a regional platform and the growing hesitation among SAARC countries to engage with one another have created a vacuum.
This vacuum is increasingly being filled by religious radicalism and internal insecurity across the region.
The road ahead remains uncertain.
The Road Ahead First, without mutual accommodation between India and Pakistan, the revival of SAARC is inconceivable.
Pakistan cannot be dismissed as a strategic entity.
All major powers, including the United States, China, Russia and Turkey, engage with Pakistan, even when India chooses to remain disengaged.
Foreign policy expert Kanti Bajpai believes that Pakistan is strategically attractive for three reasons: its location, its power and its capacity to disrupt.
With approximately half a million personnel in uniform and roughly 200 nuclear warheads, Pakistan remains India’s strategic competitor.
It reportedly possesses more nuclear warheads than India.

There is no way to peace but peace is the way.
Second, by keeping SAARC in limbo, India risks pushing even Bangladesh towards a more adversarial regional posture.
To borrow the expression of Sajeeb Wazed, son of former Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, Bangladesh risks becoming another Pakistan on India’s eastern front.
India’s former Chief of Defence Staff, General Anil Chauhan, recently observed that there could be a convergence of interests among China, Pakistan and Bangladesh.
Bangladesh’s Prime Minister, Tarique Rahman, has called for a “Bangladesh First” policy to guide his government.
He has not visited India despite an invitation from the Indian Prime Minister.
Bangladesh is also reportedly reviewing around 101 bilateral agreements with India.

India, as a major regional power, can offer ideas and solutions to the challenges confronting the region.
Genuine regional leadership demands the capacity to generate ideas, build consensus and deliver tangible solutions.
By adopting such an approach, India can enhance its regional influence and strengthen its position as a responsible regional power.
During recent India-Pakistan Track II meetings, the dangers posed by climate change got focussed attention.
Climate change can severely degrade critical sectors, including water and electricity, transportation networks and supply chains.

stories.title: Supreme Court terms vehicular emissions major contributor to air pollution in Delhi-NCR
stories.summary: The Bench highlighted the large number of vehicles plying on roads connecting Delhi with neighbouring areas, including Ghaziabad, Greater Noida, Gurugram and Faridabad

article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Friday (November 6, 2026) termed vehicular emissions a major contributor to air pollution in Delhi-NCR and said immediate, medium- and long-term measures were needed to curb the rising air quality index.

Hearing a suo motu case examining the regulatory framework governing air pollution, a Bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana also expressed concern over “bumper-to-bumper” traffic in Delhi-NCR.
“We keep talking and sometimes make statements and suggestions, but the point is that AQI is already touching 400,” the CJI said.
The Bench highlighted the large number of vehicles plying on roads connecting Delhi with neighbouring areas, including Ghaziabad, Greater Noida, Gurugram and Faridabad.
“Look at the roads in Delhi and the roads connecting Delhi with the NCR.
Take a look at any road and the kind of vehicles moving on it.
That is the major problem,” the CJI said.
The Bench said the poor people are the real sufferers, as they are on the roads, and moreover, the festival time is the only period when they earn a livelihood.
On stubble burning, the Bench stressed the need to educate farmers about using machines instead of resorting to farm fires.

On the plea seeking closure of schools or running them in hybrid mode for students of all age groups if the air quality index (AQI) rises above a certain mark, the bench said it will go by experts’ opinion.

Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati, appearing for the Centre and other authorities, referred to the regulatory framework covering five major sectors: industrial emissions, vehicular pollution, construction and demolition dust, road dust and stubble burning.

She told the Bench that several measures had been introduced, including restrictions on the entry of certain vehicles, geo-tagging of pollution under control (PUC) certificates and action against visibly polluting vehicles through complaints received on applications and social media.
